name: Femoral-Popliteal Bypass
overview: Bypass graft from femoral to popliteal artery

pimpingQuestions.question: The femoral artery develops from which embryologic vessel, and what transition occurs at the adductor hiatus?
pimpingQuestions.answer: The external iliac artery (from the 5th lumbar intersegmental artery/umbilical artery system). At the adductor hiatus (opening in adductor magnus), the superficial femoral artery becomes the popliteal artery as it enters the popliteal fossa. This transition point is the most common site of atherosclerotic occlusion in the lower extremity.

pimpingQuestions.question: What is the anatomy of the femoral triangle, and what mnemonic helps remember the contents?
pimpingQuestions.answer: Boundaries: inguinal ligament (superior), sartorius (lateral), adductor longus (medial). Floor: iliopsoas, pectineus. Contents (lateral to medial): NAVEL — Nerve, Artery, Vein, Empty space, Lymphatics. The femoral sheath encloses the artery, vein, and lymphatics but NOT the nerve (it's outside the sheath).

pimpingQuestions.question: What conduit is preferred for femoral-popliteal bypass, and why?
pimpingQuestions.answer: Autologous greater saphenous vein (reversed or in-situ) is the gold standard — 5-year primary patency 60-80% (above-knee) and 50-65% (below-knee). PTFE graft is acceptable for above-knee bypass (50-60% at 5 years) but significantly worse below-knee (30-40%). Vein is ALWAYS preferred below-knee. Preoperative vein mapping with duplex ultrasound is mandatory.

pimpingQuestions.question: What is the most common cause of early graft failure (<30 days) versus late failure (>2 years)?
pimpingQuestions.answer: Early: technical error — anastomotic stenosis, graft kinking, retained valve leaflet (in-situ), or intimal flap. Late: neointimal hyperplasia (1-24 months) at the anastomotic sites, or progression of native atherosclerotic disease (>2 years). Graft surveillance with duplex ultrasound every 3 months for the first year detects stenoses before occlusion.

pimpingQuestions.question: What is the WIfI classification system, and how does it guide limb salvage decisions?
pimpingQuestions.answer: Wound, Ischemia, and foot Infection staging: each graded 0-3. It predicts major amputation risk and benefit from revascularization. High WIfI scores (stage 4-5) predict >25% amputation risk at 1 year without intervention. It helps decide between revascularization (bypass vs endovascular) and primary amputation.
